title: Cordless drill: motor, gearbox, trigger, chuck and battery
summary: A dead cordless drill gives a 12–20 V motor with a planetary gearbox and clutch, a trigger with a built-in speed controller, a keyless chuck, and a battery pack of lithium-ion or nickel cells. Often the drill is fine and only the battery is dead: check before you strip it.

steps.text: Take the battery off. Look at it: swollen, cracked or hot packs go outdoors on bare ground (see safety_swollen_lithium).
Check whether the drill works before stripping it: connect a charged pack or a supply of the same voltage. A working drill with a dead pack is worth more whole (see notes).
Lay the drill on its side and remove every screw from the clamshell (Torx or Phillips; some are security Torx). Lift the top half off slowly and photograph how the parts sit.
Lift out the motor, gearbox and trigger together. Unplug or desolder the motor leads from the trigger only if you need them apart.
Keep the trigger switch module whole: it holds the forward/reverse switch and the speed-control MOSFET. With the motor, it is a ready-made variable-speed drive.
Pull the motor out of the back of the gearbox. The small pinion gear stays on the motor shaft.

Chuck: open the jaws fully and look inside. There is usually a screw with a left-hand thread: turn it clockwise to undo it. Then grip a hex key in the jaws and strike the key sharply anticlockwise with a hammer to unscrew the chuck.
steps.warn: Wear eye protection when striking hardened steel.

steps.text: Battery pack: undo the screws or crack the glued seam, away from the cells. Cut the leads one at a time and tape them. Separate cells as in teardown_laptop_battery.
steps.warn: A short across a power tool pack can deliver tens of amps: enough to melt wire and start a fire.

steps.text: Measure the cells. Lithium-ion: 3.6–3.7 V nominal each. Nickel cells (NiCd or NiMH): 1.2 V nominal each.
Keep the charger with the battery parts. It holds a small mains power supply and a charge board.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Motor and gearbox.** A strong, high-speed DC motor with a planetary gearbox and clutch: a winch drive, a pump drive, a grain mill or a hand-crank generator (turn the chuck, take power from the motor leads).
- **Trigger module.** A variable-speed controller rated for tens of amps at 12–20 V. Reuse it for any similar motor.
- **Chuck.** Fits onto other motors with the same shaft thread, or onto a hand brace.
- **Battery cells.** Lithium-ion packs hold 3 cells (10.8–12 V) or 5 cells (18–20 V) of 18650 or 21700 size, sometimes doubled in parallel. Older packs hold 10–15 NiCd or NiMH cells.

## Keeping a drill running without its battery

- 12 V drills run from a 12 V lead-acid battery through a fused lead. Disconnect the charger first: a battery on charge can sit at 14–15 V. Build a dummy pack from a dead pack's shell with two wires out.
- 18–20 V drills need 18–20 V: five lithium-ion cells in series, or a suitable supply. Don't feed them 24 V.
- Brushless drills need their own controller board, usually in the handle. Keep the board and motor together.

## Variations

- Nickel-cadmium packs (older, heavy, labelled NiCd or Ni-Cd) contain cadmium, which is toxic. Don't burn or crush them; keep them whole or recycle them.
- Many lithium-ion packs have a protection board inside; some leave protection to the tool.
- Impact drivers and drill-drivers share batteries and motors with their brand's other tools.

## What to leave

- The plastic clamshell, unless you need the switch or belt clip.
- Lithium cells under 2.0 V; nickel cells that leak white or green crust.
